 Christy Bieber Tue, November 3, 2026 at 8:00 AM CST 5 min read shutterstock.com Attending a four-year out-of-state school comes at a hefty cost: $31,880 per student per year on average in the U.S. Given these prices, it's not surprising that 43 million Americans have student loan debt, with total student loan debt now exceeding $1.6 trillion . 
 According to a 2026 College Savings Foundation survey , 93% of U.S. parents plan to help fund their children's higher education. With the burden that comes with educational debt, those who can get support would likely welcome it. But what happens if this financial support comes with emotional strings?

 Let's say, for example, that Rachel was married to a wealthy man named Tim. Tim was abusive, and Rachel left him and kept custody of their children. When they separated , Tim agreed to pay for their children's college education. The problem is, it's time for their daughter Joy to attend school, and Tim is ghosting Rachel rather than coming up with the cash. 
 Rachel isn't sure whether she should keep after him or give up to protect her mental health. Fortunately, lawyers and financial therapists both weighed in on this difficult situation to help shed some light on the best move. 
 Can Rachel make him pay? 
 The first big question Rachel needs to answer is whether Tim would have to pay if she pursued him. It's one thing to interact with her abuser if doing so is likely to result in her daughter getting tens of thousands of dollars. It's another to do it if there's virtually no chance Tim would actually have to pay. 
 So, can Tim be forced to fulfill his promise? 
 "It depends on what was agreed in writing," Jean Brown , a San Antonio family law attorney, told Moneywise. "In most states, parents have no automatic legal duty to pay for college. And a verbal promise, even a sincere one, is hard to enforce." 
 If Tim agreed in writing, though, that changes things. "If the promise is in the divorce decree or settlement agreement, the situation is different," Brown said. "A written college provision can generally be enforced like any other contract, and courts have enforced them, including unpaid tuition and, in some cases, attorney's fees." 
 Story Continues If there is a clause in the divorce decree, Rachel also needs to understand the scope of it and whether it's clear on Tim's duties. 
 "'He agreed to pay for college' is one of the most under-specified sentences in a divorce agreement," Liz Pharo Sauls, CEO of Divorce.com , told Moneywise. "Which school? Tuition only, or room, board, books, and fees? Capped at the in-state public rate, or whatever the kid gets into? How many years, and what if it takes five?" 
 Sauls recommended that Rachel carefully review the written record and consider talking with an attorney who can help her determine how likely she is to win.

 Should Rachel try to make him pay? 
 If Rachel believes she has a good case, the next big question is what impact pursuing it could have on her mental health. 
 "It comes down to what it will cost you in money, time, and emotional energy, and whether you have support to get through it," Justena Kavanagh , founder of NYC Counseling, told Moneywise. "For some of my clients, letting it go is real self-protection, not defeat. For others, holding the ex accountable is part of how they heal." 
 Amanda Carnesecchi , an associate therapist at Gateway to Solutions, also pointed out that it's not just Rachel's mental health at stake. "Another strong factor to consider is how this affects your child and what their relationship with the other parent looks like," she told Moneywise. If Joy has no relationship with Tim, Rachel may not want to let an abuser into their lives even if he comes bearing cash. 
 The good news is, Rachel doesn't have to take an all-or-nothing approach to the situation, according to Molly Halbrooks , a licensed marriage and family therapist and the founder of Restore Counseling. 
 "Many parents feel like the only options are 'fight for every dollar' or walk away completely," Halbrooks said. "There's usually a middle path. Let an attorney or mediator handle the communication, set a timeline for how long you'll pursue it, and decide ahead of time what 'enough' looks like." 
 This approach could help Rachel avoid destroying her mental health while still doing all she can to get college costs covered. 
 "I often talk with clients about choosing your hard," Halbrooks said. "Pursuing the money is hard. Letting it go is hard too. The goal is to choose the hard that best protects your well-being and your kids."
